planting.note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in fall or early spring in average to clay soil in full sun to light shade; California wild rose spreads readily by suckers and naturalizes along streambanks and canyon bottoms.

directions: Plant in average to heavy soil near seasonal moisture in full sun to light shade; this thicket-forming California native tolerates clay and periodic flooding better than most garden roses. Fragrant single pink blooms open in flushes from late spring through summer on arching, thorny canes, followed by small red hips that persist into winter and feed songbirds. It spreads by root suckers to form dense colonial thickets, making it well suited to streambank stabilization, wildlife hedgerows, and naturalized plantings rather than formal beds. Cut old canes to the ground periodically to renew vigor and control spread.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Arctic rose is among the most cold-hardy roses in cultivation and needs no winter protection even in severe climates.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this circumboreal species tolerates the coldest winters of any commonly available rose, surviving reliably to USDA zone 2 without dieback. Solitary, deep pink to rose-purple flowers open in late spring on densely bristled canes covered in fine, needle-like prickles, followed by pear-shaped orange-red hips that persist into winter. Native across the northern forests of Canada, Alaska, and Siberia, it is best used as a rugged wildlife hedge or naturalized planting in cold-climate gardens rather than a refined border shrub. Remove only dead or damaged canes, since flowers form on second-year and older wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; shining rose spreads by rhizomes to form a low, dense colony and suits damp meadows and bog margins.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; this diminutive northeastern species is one of the smallest wild roses in cultivation, rarely exceeding three feet, and spreads gently by rhizomes into a low colony rather than forming a large thicket. Fragrant single pink flowers open in early summer on slender canes covered in fine bristles rather than hooked thorns, and the glossy, narrow leaflets turn brilliant scarlet-orange in fall before small red hips ripen. Native to bogs, wet meadows, and rocky lakeshores from Newfoundland to New England, it performs best in consistently moist, humus-rich soil and is well suited to a rain garden or native pollinator border. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead canes in early spring.

common_name: Thérèse Bugnet Rugosa Rose (Extremely Cold-Hardy Prairie Rugosa)

planting.note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Thérèse Bugnet is a Canadian-bred rugosa hybrid selected for extreme prairie cold-hardiness.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; bred in Alberta for prairie winters, this rugosa hybrid survives extreme cold with minimal dieback and needs no winter protection. Large, loosely double, lilac-pink blooms with a strong, classic rose fragrance open in repeated flushes from late spring through fall on reddish canes that add striking winter color once leaves drop. Foliage turns shades of orange and red in autumn, extending seasonal interest beyond the bloom season typical of most rugosas. Prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since flowers form on both old and new growth.

common_name: F.J. Grootendorst Rugosa Rose (Fringed Carnation-Red Rugosa)

planting.note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; F.J. Grootendorst is a Dutch-bred rugosa hybrid grown for its unusual fringed, carnation-like flowers.

directions: Plant in average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this rugosa hybrid tolerates poor and coastal soils typical of the class while bringing an unusual flower form to the group. Small, double, bright crimson-red blooms with distinctly frilled, fringed petal edges resembling miniature carnations open in dense clusters from summer through fall, though the double flowers produce few of the large hips typical of straight rugosas. Foliage retains the rugged, deeply wrinkled texture and strong disease resistance of its rugosa parent, and the upright, twiggy habit works well as an informal flowering hedge. Prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since rugosa hybrids resent hard pruning.

common_name: Sarah Van Fleet Rugosa Rose (Tall Fragrant Pink Rugosa Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Sarah Van Fleet is a tall, vigorous rugosa hybrid well suited to the back of a hardy shrub border or informal hedge.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the tall, upright habit makes Sarah Van Fleet well suited to the back of a hardy shrub border, a tall informal hedge, or screening rather than smaller-scale rugosa uses. Semi-double, silvery-pink blooms with a strong, clove-like fragrance open in continuous flushes from late spring into fall against rugged, wrinkled rugosa foliage that stays clean without spraying. It sets few hips compared to single-flowered rugosas, since breeding emphasized repeat bloom and height over hip production. Prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since flowers form on both old and new growth.
